title: Chelsea and ‘Huddlegate’: Is Liam Rosenior focusing on the wrong issue?
content:
“I’m disappointed — there’s more focus and emphasis on the things that don’t matter,” Liam Rosenior said in his post-match press conference when questioned about referee Paul Tierney’s surreal, instantly comedic involvement in the Chelsea players’ pre-match team huddle around the centre spot against Newcastle.

Rosenior then proceeded at length to place much more focus and emphasis on the very thing that, in the grander scheme of Chelsea’s faltering season, does not matter.

“I’m going to make it really clear,” he added. “I want to protect my players. I’m respectful to the game. My players made the decision that they wanted to be around the ball, to respect the ball and show unity and leadership. That is not my decision. That was a decision between the leadership group and the team.

“There is nothing that they’re doing with that huddle that is disrespectful to the opposition. We had a meeting with the referee, my assistant goes in, and the first thing he talks about is our huddle. He says what about when I complained about Arsenal being in our half? It wasn’t the goalkeeper coach who was in our half. People who were at that game for Arsenal know why I said what I said. We’re not being disrespectful to the opposition.

“If Paul had focused more on his job, which was to make the right decisions, we would have had a penalty today. I don’t think anybody in this room can say that (Nick) Woltemade doesn’t kick Cole Palmer down in the box. So, let’s focus on the things that are important. My team showing unity is not as important as getting the decisions right on the pitch.”

Still not done, Rosenior revealed he intended to escalate the situation with Tierney’s superiors.

“I’ll be honest, I didn’t speak to Paul or his officials,” he said. “I thought it wasn’t the right thing to do. But I’ll be speaking to PGMOL. I’ll be speaking to the refs and just trying to get an understanding of why that happened.”

Rosenior’s comments — delivered less like an angry rant than an exasperated lament — were almost as bizarre to witness as the initial sight of Tierney, having pointedly refused to vacate his position on the centre spot, watching with barely concealed bemusement as Chelsea’s players closed in and locked arms around him. Cole Palmer at least acknowledged the absurdity of the situation, mischievously hugging the referee from behind and then deadpan staring at him.

It was instant top-tier meme material, and it might prove to be the funniest football moment of the year. What it did not appear to have was the slightest impact on the performance of Chelsea or their opponents on another damaging day for their hopes of qualifying for next season’s Champions League.

Chelsea players did not show much respect for the ball in the 18th minute, when they allowed Cobham graduate Tino Livramento to receive and dribble it through their first line of pressure utterly unbothered. There was no sign of unity in their defence, where Trevoh Chalobah had followed Nick Woltemade out towards the left touchline and neither Reece James nor Moises Caicedo had dropped in to properly fill the massive gap through which Joe Willock ran unchecked to lay the only goal of the game on a plate for Anthony Gordon.

There was no discernible leadership in the actions of Wesley Fofana — remarkably, at 25 years old, one of this team’s more senior players — who allowed Gordon to race past him without ever breaking into a sprint, thereby turning a likely Newcastle goal into a certain one.

Conceding one of the worst goals in recent Premier League history to lose a game might just be a bigger deal than a pre-match team huddle. In his defence, Rosenior did not shy away from admitting that Gordon’s goal was a gift, adding that it sprang from a failure of Chelsea’s press, which otherwise worked well enough to force Newcastle into long balls out of defence for most of the afternoon.

The problem with ‘Huddlegate’, as some are referring to it, is twofold. First, by committing to a ritual that creates such a sideshow ahead of each half, Chelsea’s players risk making themselves look ridiculous when, as occurred against Paris Saint-Germain and Newcastle, the team then succumb to some of the same issues that have undermined them for the best part of three years: individual errors, indiscipline, infirmity in the face of setbacks, and an inability to break through dogged, deep-lying defences.

Second, by protecting his players so vociferously on such a relatively trivial subject, Rosenior risks undermining his own credibility. That is a problem when you consider the increasingly irate atmosphere at Stamford Bridge, where just 23 of Chelsea’s 48 points in this season’s Premier League have been accumulated. The boos that reverberated around the ground at the end of each half against Newcastle felt much more substantial than the team huddles at the start.

It is easy to understand why the team huddle around the centre spot appealed to Chelsea’s players, who banded together when it mattered most to finish last season strongly under Enzo Maresca and carried the momentum into the FIFA Club World Cup. It is also easy to detect in it the influence of player support and development officer Willie Isa, who hails from the world of rugby, where ostentatious pre-match rituals and territorial domination are psychological weapons. If you intimidate or annoy your opponents in the process, so much the better.

But there is no evidence at this stage that it is helping Chelsea’s performances or results. They are almost certain to be eliminated from the Champions League at the round-of-16 stage and are on pace to end this Premier League season with 61 points, eight fewer than last year and two fewer than in 2023-24 under Mauricio Pochettino, when they finished sixth. You have to go back to 2006-07 to find the last time that tally was enough to secure fifth place.

The omens are not good, and huddling around the matchball or even a stone-faced referee is unlikely to make things better. Chelsea and Rosenior need to focus on the things that matter.
